title: What training do you need for a radiation user license in NSW?
description: What NSW requires to get a radiation user license, the approved courses for health roles, the 2025 Regulation changes, and the ARPANSA training duties.
shortAnswer: In New South Wales, the Protection from Harmful Radiation Act 1990 requires every individual who uses regulated material, such as X-ray or fluoroscopy apparatus, to hold a radiation user license from the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) unless an exemption applies. Applicants must show radiation safety knowledge and experience, usually through AHPRA registration plus an EPA approved course. The Protection from Harmful Radiation Regulation 2025 commenced on August 29, 2025 and changed several exemptions.
keyTakeaways: The license is personal: it is issued only to individuals, covers only the regulated material and purpose the holder was found competent for, and lasts 1 or 3 years.
Applicants must demonstrate knowledge of radiation safety principles and practice, relevant experience, and that they are a fit and proper person (section 5 of the Act).
Most medical license conditions combine current AHPRA registration with completion of a course on the EPA approved list, for example the IA22 fluoroscopy condition for specialists.
Medical registrars who use fluoroscopy outside six exempt specialties needed a license by May 29, 2026, and management license holders needed a radiation management plan by September 1, 2026.
The ARPANSA Code for Radiation Protection in Medical Exposure (RPS C-5) makes the facility's Responsible Person keep a named list of trained staff and records of radiation protection training.
regulator: NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA), applying codes published by the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA)
appliesTo: Individuals who use radioactive substances, ionizing radiation apparatus, prescribed non-ionizing apparatus or sealed source devices in NSW
Radiographers, radiation therapists, nuclear medicine staff, radiologists and medical specialists who use fluoroscopy
General practitioners, physiotherapists and registered nurses who perform restricted radiography, typically in rural and remote sites
Hospitals, imaging practices and other radiation management license holders responsible for regulated material

sections.heading: Who needs a radiation user license in NSW?

blocks.text: Any individual who uses regulated material in NSW must hold a radiation user license and comply with its conditions, unless a regulation exempts them. The EPA's [user license introduction](https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/Your-environment/Radiation/radiation-user-licence/user-licence-introduction) defines regulated material as radioactive substances, ionizing radiation apparatus, prescribed non-ionizing radiation apparatus and sealed source devices, and says "to use" includes to operate, possess for use, handle or manipulate.

Three features shape how employers manage the obligation. The license is issued only to natural persons, not companies. It authorizes only the regulated material and purpose for which the holder was found competent. And it is valid for either 1 or 3 years. The EPA lists occupations that may need a license, including dental practitioners, medical specialists using fluoroscopy, nuclear medicine physicians, nurses and general practitioners working as remote operators, medical radiographers, radiation therapists and veterinarians.

A separate radiation management license is held by the person or organization responsible for the regulated material, usually the hospital, imaging practice or clinic. Both layers matter for training: the user license proves the individual's entry competence, and the management license holder is accountable for supervision, radiation management plans and the workplace safety rules. Readers working through broader workplace duties should also see the [WHS duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training).

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects NSW EPA and ARPANSA material as at November 2026. The EPA's licensing pages were updated in September 2025 after the 2025 Regulation commenced, and the IA22R criteria were amended after the Radiation Advisory Council met in May 2026. Confirm license conditions on the EPA criteria page before applying.

sections.heading: What knowledge and training does the EPA require before granting a license?

blocks.text: Applicants must demonstrate appropriate knowledge of the principles and practices of radiation safety and protection, experience applicable to the proposed activities, and that they are a fit and proper person under section 5 of the Act. The EPA's [user license criteria page](https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/Your-environment/Radiation/radiation-user-licence/user-licence-introduction/user-licence-criteria) translates that into condition codes, each with its own prerequisites, and says complete applications that meet the criteria are usually approved within 14 working days.

Applicants who cannot show the set criteria, for example those with overseas qualifications or experience in place of a listed course, are assessed case by case. The EPA may refer them to the Radiation Advisory Council, which takes 10 to 12 weeks and attracts a higher fee. Many listed courses carry a "completed prior to" date, meaning older completions are accepted but the course is no longer offered as a current route, so credentialing staff should check completion dates, not just course names.

blocks.text: The pattern is consistent: professional registration with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) establishes the clinical baseline, and the EPA approved course supplies the radiation safety element. Registration itself carries separate continuing professional development duties, covered in [Ahpra CPD registration standards](/regulations/ahpra-cpd-registration-standards).

sections.heading: What changed under the Protection from Harmful Radiation Regulation 2025?

blocks.text: The 2025 Regulation replaced the 2013 Regulation on August 29, 2025 and moved several groups into or out of licensing. According to the EPA's [summary of the changes](https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/Your-environment/Radiation/managing-radiation-nsw/changes-regulation-radiation), it provides for exemptions and course approvals, prescribes workplace safety rules and incident reporting, and increases penalties.

items: **Medical registrars:** registrars are exempt only in dermatology, radiology, nuclear medicine, ophthalmology, radiation oncology and rheumatology, subject to supervision. Registrars in other specialties, such as cardiology or vascular surgery, who use fluoroscopy had until May 29, 2026 to complete a course and obtain a license.

**Dental practitioners:** from December 1, 2025, registered dental practitioners are also exempt for orthopantomogram (OPG) and lateral cephalometric apparatus, so a license is needed only for cone beam computed tomography. Dental assistants gain the same exemption if they complete an EPA approved course and work under general supervision. Wider dental training duties are covered in [dental infection control training](/regulations/dental-practice-infection-control-training-australia).

**Supervision moves in house:** written exemption approvals from a qualified person are no longer required. Instead, the management license holder must make sure each exempt person meets the exemption conditions and is supervised as the exemption requires.

**Radiation management plans:** every management license holder responsible for regulated material must prepare or adopt and implement a plan meeting the ARPANSA Planned Exposure Code and any relevant practice code, with a deadline of September 1, 2026.
**Incident reporting:** "radiation accidents" became "radiation incidents" with new thresholds, and for certain incidents a medical physicist must estimate the dose received.

blocks.text: In May 2026, after a Radiation Advisory Council meeting, the EPA removed the requirement for IA22R applicants to show acceptance into an Australian Medical Council approved program and added supervision requirements to IA22R conditions.

sections.heading: What does the ARPANSA Medical Exposure Code require of training?

blocks.text: The [Code for Radiation Protection in Medical Exposure (2019) (RPS C-5)](https://www.arpansa.gov.au/regulation-and-licensing/regulatory-publications/radiation-protection-series/codes-and-standards/rpsc-5) puts the training duty on the facility's Responsible Person, not on the individual alone. Clause 3.5.2 requires that radiological medical practitioners, operators, medical physicists, radiopharmaceutical scientists and other personnel with duties for patient radiation protection are specialized in the appropriate area, meet the education, training and competence requirements of the relevant regulator, are named on an up to date list referenced in the Radiation Management Plan, and hold a use license where one is required.

The Code also requires the Responsible Person to "document the induction and training programs specific to patient radiation protection" and record participation, and to keep personnel training records for seven years or as otherwise specified by the regulator. Schedule A says the Radiation Management Plan must address the training, qualifications and competencies of people with patient protection responsibilities and their induction and ongoing training.

These codes bind NSW licensees because the states agreed the [National Directory for Radiation Protection](https://www.arpansa.gov.au/regulation-and-licensing/regulatory-publications/national-directory-for-radiation-protection) (2nd edition, 2021), endorsed by all state and territory health ministers between July and October 2021. The EPA says it adopted the codes listed in that edition in 2022 and that adopted codes take legal effect as license and exemption conditions. Its [list of adopted documents](https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/Your-environment/Radiation/radiation-codes-adopted-epa) includes RPS C-5 and notes that the 2025 Dental Code is not yet in the National Directory.

blocks.text: Credentialing committees can fold the license check into scope of practice decisions, so that a clinician is not granted fluoroscopy privileges without a matching license condition. That approach is described in [credentialing and scope of clinical practice](/regulations/credentialing-and-scope-of-clinical-practice-australia), and the [training records audit guide](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers register design.

sections.heading: How do renewal and interstate recognition work?

blocks.text: A user license must be renewed on or within 60 days after its expiry date, and once that window passes the holder must apply for a new license. The EPA's [renewals page](https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/Your-environment/Radiation/radiation-user-licence/user-licence-introduction/user-licence-renewals-variations) warns that a new application may need fresh proof of qualifications, particularly where the license depends on current professional registration or the criteria have changed. Regulated material must not be used while the license has lapsed.

Since December 1, 2022, a person holding a current radiation user license in another state or territory, other than Queensland, may be able to work in NSW under automatic mutual recognition after notifying the EPA. Employers should still check that the interstate license covers the same practice, because a recognized license does not widen the holder's scope. The [refresh cycle guide](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) explains how to schedule license expiry alerts alongside internal refresher training.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents each license condition, exemption class and RPS C-5 duty as a node linked to the roles and equipment it governs. When the EPA amends a condition, as it did for IA22R in 2026, the affected clinicians, supervision rules and evidence requirements can be traced directly rather than found by searching course catalogs.

faqs.q: Do nurses in NSW need a license to take X-rays?
faqs.a: Registered nurses who take restricted diagnostic X-rays, usually in rural or remote facilities without a radiographer, need the IA14R condition. It requires current AHPRA registration and completion of an approved course, such as the Health Education and Training Institute "NSW Limited licence radiography course".

faqs.q: Do dentists still need a NSW radiation license?
faqs.a: From December 1, 2025, registered dental practitioners are exempt for intraoral imaging, OPG and lateral cephalometric apparatus when they comply with the ARPANSA Dental Code and the Regulation. A license is still required for cone beam computed tomography.

faqs.q: Is there a continuing education requirement to renew a NSW user license?
faqs.a: The EPA renewal page does not set a refresher course for renewal. However, renewal can require fresh evidence where a license depends on current professional registration or criteria have changed, and RPS C-5 expects ongoing training documented in the Radiation Management Plan.

faqs.q: Who maintains the list of trained staff in a hospital imaging department?
faqs.a: Under RPS C-5 the Responsible Person, normally the management license holder, must keep an up to date list of personnel with patient radiation protection duties and reference it in the Radiation Management Plan, along with training records.

faqs.q: What if a medical registrar used fluoroscopy before the 2025 Regulation?
faqs.a: Registrars outside dermatology, radiology, nuclear medicine, ophthalmology, radiation oncology and rheumatology who use fluoroscopy had until May 29, 2026 to complete an approved course and obtain the IA22R license condition. After that date, use without a license or an exemption is not permitted.

factCheck.claim: Individuals who use regulated material must hold a radiation user licence under the Protection from Harmful Radiation Act 1990 and Regulation 2025; licences issue only to natural persons, cover only material and purposes found competent for, and are valid for 1 or 3 years

Applicants must demonstrate knowledge of radiation safety principles and practices, applicable experience, and be fit and proper (section 5 of the Act); complete applications usually approved within 14 working days; case by case referrals to the Radiation Advisory Council take 10 to 12 weeks

IA14R requires AHPRA registration as medical practitioner, physiotherapist or registered nurse plus an approved course (HETI NSW limited licence radiography course); IA22 requires AHPRA specialist registration plus approved fluoroscopy course; IA22R criteria amended after the May 2026 Radiation Advisory Council meeting to remove the AMC approved program requirement

Protection from Harmful Radiation Regulation 2025 commenced 29 August 2025 replacing the 2013 Regulation; registrars exempt only in six specialties and others using fluoroscopy must be licensed by 29 May 2026; dental OPG and lateral ceph exemption from 1 December 2025, licence still needed for CBCT; radiation management plans due 1 September 2026; written exemption approvals no longer required

RPS C-5 clause 3.5.2 requires personnel with patient radiation protection duties to be specialised, meet regulator training and competence requirements, be named on a list referenced in the Radiation Management Plan, and hold a use licence where required; induction and training programs documented with participation recorded; personnel training records kept seven years
NDRP 2nd edition endorsed by all state and territory health ministers between July and October 2021

EPA adopted the codes in the second edition of the National Directory in 2022, including RPS C-5; adopted codes have legal effect as licence and exemption conditions; 2025 Dental Code not yet in the National Directory
User licence must be renewed on or within 60 days after expiry; automatic mutual recognition from 1 December 2022 for licences from other states and territories except Queensland
